outputs.jobspec:
#!/bin/bash

# SBATCH Directives

# Set the job name
#SBATCH --job-name=lammps_hns

# Request 1 compute node
# This is equivalent to the -N1 in the flux command.
#SBATCH --nodes=1

# Request 64 tasks. Since we are on a single 64-core node, this allocates one task per core.
# This is equivalent to the -n 64 in the flux command.
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64

# Request exclusive access to the node.
# This is a performance optimization that prevents other jobs from running on the same node,
# ensuring that your application has access to all resources (memory bandwidth, cache, etc.).
#SBATCH --exclusive

# Bind tasks to cores.
# This is another performance optimization that pins each MPI task to a specific CPU core.
# It prevents the operating system from moving tasks around, which improves cache performance.
#SBATCH --cpu-bind=cores

# Specify the output and error files. %j is replaced with the job ID.
#SBATCH --output=lammps-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=lammps-%j.err

# --- Job Execution ---

# Print the start time
echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# Run the lammps executable using srun.
# srun is Slurm's command for launching parallel jobs and it will automatically
# distribute the 64 tasks according to the SBATCH directives above.
# The arguments to lmp are passed directly.
srun lmp -v x 20 -v y 20 -v z 20 -in in.reaxff.hns

# Print the end time
echo "End time:" $( date +%s )

#!/bin/bash

#SBATCH --nodes=2                # Number of nodes requested, same as -N2 in flux.
#SBATCH --ntasks=128               # Total number of tasks for the job, same as -n128 in flux.
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64       # Explicitly set 64 tasks per node (128 tasks / 2 nodes).

# The --exclusive flag requests dedicated nodes for the job. This prevents
# other jobs from running on the same nodes, eliminating resource contention
# for CPU, memory, and network bandwidth, which is critical for performance.
#SBATCH --exclusive

# The --cpu-bind=cores directive pins each task to a specific CPU core.
# This improves performance by enhancing data locality (reducing cache misses) and
# minimizing task migration overhead, which is beneficial for compute-bound codes.
#SBATCH --cpu-bind=cores

# The --distribution=block:block directive controls how tasks are mapped to nodes.
# Using 'block' ensures that consecutive MPI ranks are placed on the same node,
# which can improve performance for applications with high intra-node communication.
#SBATCH --distribution=block:block

# Record the start time of the job execution.
echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# The srun command is Slurm's equivalent of mpirun or flux run for launching parallel tasks.
# It automatically uses the resources allocated by the SBATCH directives.
srun lmp -v x 20 -v y 20 -v z 20 -in in.reaxff.hns

#SBATCH --ntasks=192

#SBATCH --cpu-bind=cores

#!/bin/bash

# SBATCH Directives
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Request 5 nodes for the job. This is a direct translation from the 'flux -N5' command.
#SBATCH --nodes=5

# Request a total of 320 tasks. This is a direct translation from the 'flux -n 320' command.
#SBATCH --ntasks=320

# Specify that each of the 5 nodes should run 64 tasks (320 tasks / 5 nodes).
# This ensures an even distribution of work and can improve performance by preventing
# task migration and ensuring resource allocation is predictable.
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64

# Give the job a descriptive name for easier tracking in the queue.
#SBATCH --job-name=lammps_reaxff

# Request exclusive access to the nodes. This prevents other jobs from running on the
# same nodes, which can significantly improve performance and reproducibility by
# eliminating resource contention (CPU, memory, network bandwidth).
#SBATCH --exclusive

# Request that the allocated nodes be contiguous. For tightly-coupled MPI applications
# like LAMMPS, this can reduce network latency between tasks, especially when using
# high-performance interconnects like AWS EFA.
#SBATCH --contiguous

# Bind tasks to specific CPU cores. This prevents the operating system from migrating
# tasks between cores, which improves cache utilization and overall performance.
#SBATCH --cpu-bind=cores
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Echo the start time for benchmarking purposes.
echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# Run the LAMMPS simulation using srun.
# srun is Slurm's tool for launching parallel tasks. It will automatically use the
# resources allocated by the #SBATCH directives above.
srun lmp -v x 20 -v y 20 -v z 20 -in in.reaxff.hns

# Echo the end time for benchmarking purposes.
echo "End time:" $( date +%s )

#!/bin/bash
#

#SBATCH --nodes=2              # Equivalent to Flux -N2
#SBATCH --ntasks=128           # Equivalent to Flux -n128

# This directive binds each task to a specific CPU core, which is the Slurm
# equivalent of Flux's `-o cpu-affinity=per-task` option. This improves
# performance by preventing task migration and maximizing CPU cache utilization.

# 128 tasks on 2 nodes, this places 64 tasks on the first node and 64 on the
# second. This can improve inter-process communication efficiency.
#SBATCH --distribution=block:block

# This ensures that the allocated nodes are used exclusively by this job,
# preventing interference from other jobs and providing consistent performance.
#SBATCH --exclusive

# -- Job Execution --

# srun is the Slurm command to launch parallel tasks. It automatically uses
# the resources defined in the #SBATCH directives above.
srun lmp -v x 20 -v y 20 -v z 20 -in in.reaxff.hns

#!/bin/bash

#

#
# Output file: Where to save the job's standard output. %j is the job ID.

#
# Number of nodes: Matches the -N3 from the flux command.

#
# Number of tasks per node: Calculated from the total tasks (192) and nodes (3).
# This ensures an even distribution of 64 tasks on each node.
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64
#
# Exclusive access: Requests exclusive access to the nodes. This prevents other jobs
# from running on the same nodes, which is crucial for performance-sensitive applications.

# '-o cpu-affinity=per-task' and improves performance by enhancing cache efficiency.
#SBATCH --cpu-bind=cores
#

# this can improve performance by balancing communication load across the network fabric.
#SBATCH --distribution=cyclic:cyclic

echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# The srun command is Slurm's parallel job launcher.
# It automatically uses the resources allocated by the SBATCH directives above.
srun lmp -v x 20 -v y 20 -v z 20 -in in.reaxff.hns

The change from `pmi2` to `pmix` may improve job startup time and scalability, but it assumes the MPI library used to compile the application supports it. #!/bin/bash

# Slurm Directives
# ----------------

# Set the job name for easy identification
#SBATCH --job-name=amg_benchmark

# Request 1 compute node. This corresponds to the '-N1' in the flux command.
#SBATCH --nodes=1

# Request 64 tasks on the node. This corresponds to the '-n 64' in the flux command.
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64

# PERFORMANCE: Request exclusive access to the node. This is a best practice
# for performance-sensitive applications as it prevents other jobs from
# competing for resources like memory bandwidth and network.
#SBATCH --exclusive

# Define the output and error file names, using the job ID (%j) for uniqueness.
#SBATCH --output=amg_output_%j.log
#SBATCH --error=amg_error_%j.log

# -- End of Slurm Directives --


# Echo the start time in Unix epoch format for easy calculation
echo "Start time:" $(date +%s)

# Launch the parallel application using srun.
# --cpu-bind=cores: PERFORMANCE: This option binds each task to a physical CPU core.
# This prevents the OS from moving tasks between cores, which improves
# cache performance and reduces execution time variability.
# --mpi=pmix: PERFORMANCE: This specifies the PMIx library for process management.
# PMIx is a modern standard that is generally more performant and scalable than PMI2,
# which was requested in the original flux command.
srun --cpu-bind=cores --mpi=pmix amg -problem 2 -n 90 90 90 -P 4 4 4


# Echo the end time in Unix epoch format
echo "End time:" $(date +%s)

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --nodes=2
#SBATCH --ntasks=128
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64
#SBATCH --job-name=amg_job
#SBATCH --exclusive

# These sbatch options are added to improve performance.

#              preventing other jobs from causing interference.
# --ntasks-per-node: Helps the scheduler make better placement decisions.

echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# --cpu-bind=cores: This is a performance optimization that binds each task
#                   (MPI rank) to a specific CPU core. This can improve
#                   performance by preventing tasks from migrating between
#                   cores and improving cache utilization.
srun --cpu-bind=cores amg -problem 2 -n 90 90 90 -P 4 8 4

echo "End time:" $( date +%s )

#!/bin/bash

# Slurm Directives
#SBATCH --nodes=3
#SBATCH --ntasks=192
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64
#SBATCH --job-name=amg_job
#SBATCH --exclusive
#SBATCH --distribution=block:block

# --ntasks=192: Request a total of 192 tasks, same as the original Flux command's -n 192.
# --ntasks-per-node=64: Explicitly specify 64 tasks per node (192 tasks / 3 nodes). This helps with process placement and can improve performance.
# --job-name=amg_job: Give the job a descriptive name.
# --exclusive: Request exclusive access to the nodes to prevent other jobs from running on the same nodes and interfering with performance.
# --distribution=block:block: Distribute tasks to nodes in blocks. This can improve performance for applications with nearest-neighbor communication patterns by placing communicating tasks closer to each other.

echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# The srun command is used to launch the parallel application.
# The --mpi=pmix option tells Slurm to use the PMIx library for MPI support,
# which is a modern and performant choice for process management in MPI jobs.
srun --mpi=pmix amg -problem 2 -n 90 90 90 -P 3 8 8

echo "End time:" $( date +%s )

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=amg_benchmark
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks=256

# Performance and Distribution Directives

# We have 256 tasks on 4 nodes, so we explicitly ask for 64 tasks per node.
# This ensures an even distribution.
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64

# Distributes tasks cyclically across nodes and then cyclically across cores on each node.
# This can improve performance for applications with communication imbalances by spreading ranks across the network fabric (like EFA).
#SBATCH --distribution=cyclic:cyclic

# Bind each task to a single CPU core. This prevents tasks from migrating between cores,
# which can improve cache performance and reduce jitter.
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1

# Specifies the use of the PMI2 interface for MPI, matching the original Flux command.
# This ensures compatibility with the MPI library being used if it requires PMI2.
#SBATCH --mpi=pmi2

echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# The srun command launches the parallel application across the allocated resources.
srun amg -problem 2 -n 90 90 90 -P 4 8 8

echo "End time:" $( date +%s )

#!/bin/bash

# Slurm Job Directives

# --nodes=5: Specifies the same number of nodes as the original Flux command (-N5).
#SBATCH --nodes=5

# --ntasks-per-node=64: We have 320 tasks total (-n 320) and 5 nodes, so we request 64 tasks per node.
# This helps the scheduler place the job efficiently. The hpc7g.6xlarge instances have 64 cores,
# so this maps one task to each available core.
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64

# --job-name: Provides a descriptive name for the job in the queue.
#SBATCH --job-name=amg_benchmark

# --exclusive: Requests exclusive access to the allocated nodes. This is crucial for performance
# benchmarks as it prevents other jobs from interfering and causing resource contention.
#SBATCH --exclusive

# --output: Specifies the output file name, including the job ID (%j) for uniqueness.
#SBATCH --output=amg_output_%j.txt

# Start Timer
echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# Run the application using srun
# --cpu-bind=cores: This is a key performance optimization. It binds each MPI task to a specific CPU core,
# preventing the operating system from migrating tasks between cores. This improves cache utilization
# and reduces context switching, leading to better performance for HPC applications.
srun --cpu-bind=cores amg -problem 2 -n 90 90 90 -P 4 8 10

# End Timer
echo "End time:" $( date +%s )

#!/bin/bash

# Slurm job directives
# Request 4 nodes for the job
#SBATCH --nodes=4
# Request 256 total tasks/processes
#SBATCH --ntasks=256
# Distribute 64 tasks to each of the 4 nodes
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64
# Name the job for easier tracking
#SBATCH --job-name=amg_benchmark
# Specify output and error files
#SBATCH --output=amg_benchmark.out
#SBATCH --error=amg_benchmark.err

# --- Performance Tuning Directives ---

# --cpu-bind=per-task: Binds each task to a specific CPU core. This is the direct analog
# of Flux's 'cpu-affinity=per-task' and is crucial for preventing tasks from migrating
# between cores, which can hurt cache performance.
#SBATCH --cpu-bind=per-task

# --distribution=block:block: Distributes tasks to nodes in blocks and assigns tasks
# to cores within a node in blocks. For MPI applications, this can improve performance
# by placing communicating tasks closer together, potentially on the same NUMA node.
#SBATCH --distribution=block:block

# --exclusive: Requests exclusive access to the allocated nodes. This prevents other jobs
# from running on the same nodes, ensuring consistent performance for benchmarking by
# eliminating resource contention.
#SBATCH --exclusive

# Record the start time of the execution
echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# Run the application using srun
# srun is Slurm's tool for launching parallel jobs. It automatically propagates
# the resource requests from the #SBATCH directives to the job step.
# We are using Slurm's default MPI integration (typically PMIx), which is generally
# recommended for modern HPC systems over the older PMI2 requested in the Flux command.
srun amg -problem 2 -n 90 90 90 -P 4 8 8

# Record the end time of the execution
echo "End time:" $( date +%s )

#!/bin/bash

#SBATCH --job-name=kripke_performance_run
#SBATCH --nodes=2
#SBATCH --ntasks=128

# This directive ensures that tasks are distributed evenly across the nodes.
# With 128 tasks and 2 nodes, this allocates 64 tasks per node.
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=64

# This directive allocates the nodes for exclusive use by this job,
# preventing other jobs from running on them. This can lead to more
# consistent performance for tightly-coupled MPI applications.
#SBATCH --exclusive

# Standard output and error files
#SBATCH --output=kripke_output_%j.log
#SBATCH --error=kripke_error_%j.log

# Record the start time for benchmarking
echo "Start time:" $( date +%s )

# Launch the parallel application using srun

Usage: sbatch [OPTIONS(0)...] [ : [OPTIONS(N)...]] script(0) [args(0)...]

Parallel run options:
  -a, --array=indexes         job array index values
  -A, --account=name          charge job to specified account
      --bb=<spec>             burst buffer specifications
      --bbf=<file_name>       burst buffer specification file
  -b, --begin=time            defer job until HH:MM MM/DD/YY
      --comment=name          arbitrary comment
      --cpu-freq=min[-max[:gov]] requested cpu frequency (and governor)
  -c, --cpus-per-task=ncpus   number of cpus required per task
  -d, --dependency=type:jobid[:time] defer job until condition on jobid is satisfied
      --deadline=time         remove the job if no ending possible before
                              this deadline (start > (deadline - time[-min]))
      --delay-boot=mins       delay boot for desired node features
  -D, --chdir=directory       set working directory for batch script
  -e, --error=err             file for batch script's standard error
      --export[=names]        specify environment variables to export
      --export-file=file|fd   specify environment variables file or file
                              descriptor to export
      --get-user-env          load environment from local cluster
      --gid=group_id          group ID to run job as (user root only)
      --gres=list             required generic resources per node
      --gres-flags=opts       flags related to GRES management
  -H, --hold                  submit job in held state
      --ignore-pbs            Ignore #PBS and #BSUB options in the batch script
  -i, --input=in              file for batch script's standard input
  -J, --job-name=jobname      name of job
  -k, --no-kill               do not kill job on node failure
  -L, --licenses=names        required license, comma separated
  -M, --clusters=names        Comma separated list of clusters to issue
                              commands to.  Default is current cluster.
                              Name of 'all' will submit to run on all clusters.
                              NOTE: SlurmDBD must up.
      --container             Path to OCI container bundle
      --container-id          OCI container ID
  -m, --distribution=type     distribution method for processes to nodes
                              (type = block|cyclic|arbitrary)
      --mail-type=type        notify on state change: BEGIN, END, FAIL or ALL
      --mail-user=user        who to send email notification for job state
                              changes
      --mcs-label=mcs         mcs label if mcs plugin mcs/group is used
  -n, --ntasks=ntasks         number of tasks to run
      --nice[=value]          decrease scheduling priority by value
      --no-requeue            if set, do not permit the job to be requeued
      --ntasks-per-node=n     number of tasks to invoke on each node
  -N, --nodes=N               number of nodes on which to run (N = min[-max])
      --oom-kill-step[=0|1]   set the OOMKillStep behaviour
  -o, --output=out            file for batch script's standard output
  -O, --overcommit            overcommit resources
  -p, --partition=partition   partition requested
      --parsable              outputs only the jobid and cluster name (if present),
                              separated by semicolon, only on successful submission.
      --power=flags           power management options
      --priority=value        set the priority of the job to value
      --profile=value         enable acct_gather_profile for detailed data
                              value is all or none or any combination of
                              energy, lustre, network or task
      --propagate[=rlimits]   propagate all [or specific list of] rlimits
  -q, --qos=qos               quality of service
  -Q, --quiet                 quiet mode (suppress informational messages)
      --reboot                reboot compute nodes before starting job
      --requeue[=expedited]   if set, permit the job to be requeued
  -s, --oversubscribe         over subscribe resources with other jobs
  -S, --core-spec=cores       count of reserved cores
      --signal=[[R][B]:]num[@time] send signal when time limit within time seconds
      --spread-job            spread job across as many nodes as possible
      --spread-segments       spread job segments across separate base blocks
      --switches=max-switches{@max-time-to-wait}
                              Optimum switches and max time to wait for optimum
      --thread-spec=threads   count of reserved threads
  -t, --time=minutes          time limit
      --time-min=minutes      minimum time limit (if distinct)
      --tres-bind=...         task to tres binding options
      --tres-per-task=list    list of tres required per task
      --uid=user_id           user ID to run job as (user root only)
      --use-min-nodes         if a range of node counts is given, prefer the

  -v, --verbose               verbose mode (multiple -v's increase verbosity)
  -W, --wait                  wait for completion of submitted job
      --wckey=wckey           wckey to run job under
      --wrap[=command string] wrap command string in a sh script and submit

Constraint options:
      --cluster-constraint=[!]list specify a list of cluster constraints
      --contiguous            demand a contiguous range of nodes
  -C, --constraint=list       specify a list of constraints
  -F, --nodefile=filename     request a specific list of hosts
      --mem=MB                minimum amount of real memory
      --mincpus=n             minimum number of logical processors (threads)
                              per node
      --reservation=name      allocate resources from named reservation
      --tmp=MB                minimum amount of temporary disk
  -w, --nodelist=hosts...     request a specific list of hosts
  -x, --exclude=hosts...      exclude a specific list of hosts

Consumable resources related options:
      --exclusive[=user]      allocate nodes in exclusive mode when
